content.title: About
content.content: Chilaquiles is a traditional Mexican dish made from corn tortillas that are fried until crisp and then bathed in a sauce of tomatoes, chilies and spices. It is often served with chicken, cheese, sour cream, onion and avocado. The dish combines a flavorful sauce, crunchy texture and tender toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chilaquiles are commonly considered a Mexican breakfast and are served from early morning until lunch.
There are several regional variations: in Yucatán a green tomatillo salsa (salsa verde) is used, while central states favor a red tomato‑chili sauce.
Traditional recipes fry the tortillas first, then briefly simmer them in the sauce so they absorb flavor while staying slightly crunchy.
The dish is often topped with poached or fried eggs, and served with beans and rice as sides.
Chilaquiles originated in colonial Mexico when Spaniards introduced corn tortillas and new spices.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Tortillas and sauce provide thiamine, niacin and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and chilies are high in lycopene and vitamin C, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Corn tortillas add fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with minimal oil, chilaquiles can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: High protein when meat is added
items.content: Chicken, beef or turkey added to the dish increase its protein content.

items.title: Spicy heat level
items.content: The sauce can be very hot; people with sensitive stomachs should reduce the amount of chili.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain a lot of salt, which may be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to corn products, including tortillas.

items.title: Calorie density with cheese and sour cream
items.content: Adding cheese, sour cream or fried avocado increases the dish’s calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilaquiles hot, drenched in sauce, topped with grated cheese, a dollop of sour cream, sliced onion, avocado and fresh cilantro. They can be enjoyed as a main dish or alongside rice and beans.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to keep the sauce from drying out. They can be frozen for up to 1 month, though tortilla texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Whiskey and ginger ale is a classic highball cocktail that blends the warm, caramel notes of bourbon or Scotch with the crisp, spicy fizz of ginger ale. It is typically served over ice in a tall glass, garnished with a lime wedge or a sprig of mint.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink emerged in the United States in the early 1920s when ginger ale became a popular non‑alcoholic beverage.
Originally, ginger ale was marketed as a medicinal tonic for nausea and colds.
In English‑speaking countries the cocktail is often simply called a “Whiskey Ginger.”
The combination of whiskey’s sweetness and ginger’s bite accentuates flavors such as vanilla, caramel, and spice.
The recipe is versatile – you can swap bourbon for Irish or Canadian whiskey, or use homemade ginger syrup topped with soda water.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Ginger is known to stimulate gastric juices and help relieve mild digestive upset.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Whiskey contains polyphenols that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: Moderate alcohol consumption can promote relaxation and lower anxiety levels.

items.title: Alcohol effects
items.content: Excessive whiskey intake increases the risk of liver disease, cardiovascular problems, and dependence.

items.title: Sugar content in ginger ale
items.content: Most commercial ginger ales are high in sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Ginger allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to ginger, including skin itching and swelling.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Pour 50 ml of whiskey over ice in a highball glass, add 150‑200 ml of ginger ale, and stir gently. Garnish with a lime wedge or a mint sprig if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the whiskey bottle in a cool, dark place with the cap tightly sealed. Keep opened ginger ale refrigerated to maintain carbonation and freshness.
